title: Amoghavarsha Opens Kannada's Royal Path
subtitle: When Rashtrakuta Royal Power Turned to the Music of Kannada Words
moral: A language flourishes when scholars teach it how to sing.

sources.citation: Kavirajamarga, c. 850 CE, ed. R. Narasimhachar (1926)
sources.note: Primary poetics text associated with Amoghavarsha and Sri Vijaya.

sources.citation: Nilgund inscription of Amoghavarsha and Sanjan Copper Plates, Epigraphia Indica / CII Vol. IV
sources.note: Primary epigraphic anchors for Amoghavarsha's reign and patronage.

sources.citation: Sheldon Pollock, The Language of the Gods in the World of Men (2006)
sources.note: Recent influential account of Kannada's 'literization' and regional literary culture.

panels.shot: sweeping royal wide from slightly low angle

dialogue.text: In Rashtrakuta Manyakheta, Amoghavarsha I and poet Sri Vijaya shape Kavirajamarga, giving Kannada a royal path beside the ancient power of Sanskrit.

panels.shot: wide aerial view of Deccan landscape

dialogue.text: By the ninth century, the Deccan is a web of powers and tongues. Rashtrakutas rule from Manyakheta, while temples, courts and markets echo in Sanskrit, Prakrit and many local Kannada voices.
Amoghavarsha, who inherited an empire of steel and stone, turns his gaze to learning. In his hall, Sanskrit pundits and Kannada scholars meet under the same royal eye.
Across India, kings have long used Sanskrit, the language of gods and learned men. But Amoghavarsha and his poet Sri Vijaya dream of a court where Kannada too can carry royal thought.

panels.shot: slow push-in on map of Karnataka

dialogue.text: “Mahārāja, there is already a country of Kannada speech. It needs a path.”

panels.shot: intimate study interior, warm lamp light

dialogue.text: Together, king and poet begin Kavirajamarga, a ‘Royal Path for Poets’ in Kannada—Sri Vijaya leading the craft, Amoghavarsha lending authority, guidance and a patron’s steady light.

panels.shot: close-up on a palm leaf being inscribed

dialogue.text: Kavirajamarga does not begin Kannada poetry. It gathers scattered practice, names meters and styles, and teaches poets how to shape sound, image and meaning with care.

panels.shot: medium shot of both reading aloud

dialogue.text: “Let Kannada walk beside Sanskrit, not behind it.”
The treatise praises earlier Kannada masters—names preserved, works vanished. It proves a living tradition already existed, and honors those whose songs now survive only by memory.
When Kavirajamarga is ready, it is not hidden in a scholar’s corner. It is announced in the Rashtrakuta court, so poets and officials across Kannada lands hear the king’s endorsement.

dialogue.speaker: amoghavarsha_i_and_sri_vijaya
dialogue.text: “Let every learned man know: Kannada has its own royal way of poetry.”
Inscriptions like Nilgund and the Sanjan plates show Amoghavarsha’s reign: land grants, Jain patronage, and a court where the king’s fame is sung in both Sanskrit and Kannada.

panels.shot: medium shot of scribes copying manuscripts

dialogue.text: From Manyakheta, copies travel to temple schools and poet’s houses. Kavirajamarga becomes a guidebook for craft, giving structure to a Kannada literary world spread across regions.
Sri Vijaya knows this work is only a beginning. Rules can guide, but they cannot replace imagination. The path is laid; each poet must walk it differently.
In centuries to come, great Kannada poets will rise. Their works differ in faith and style, but all inherit a sense that their language deserves rules, respect and a kingdom of its own.
The king is remembered for peace‑making, patronage of Jain teachers, and gentle rule. Kavirajamarga adds another mark: a ruler who saw power in the shaping of words, not only in weapons.

panels.shot: final close-up of open palm-leaf manuscript

dialogue.text: Amoghavarsha and Sri Vijaya did not invent Kannada song, but they gave it a royal path. Their work shows how a language flourishes when scholars teach it how to sing with discipline and pride.
